webTitle: Republican senator criticizes White House for taxpayer-funded Trump ads

fields.headline: Republican senator criticizes White House for taxpayer-funded Trump ads
fields.trailText: John Kennedy pushes back against such spending as pro-Trump ‘public service announcements’ air before midterms
fields.bodyText: As the White House expands a taxpayer-funded advertising campaign to promote Donald Trump’s political agenda before the November midterm elections, Senator John Kennedy told CBS News on Sunday “there ought to be a rule” against such spending – before tacitly admitting such spending is “probably” illegal. Kennedy, the US president’s fellow Republican, was asked by Margaret Brennan, the CBS Face the Nation host, about the White House spending to air multiple ads featuring Trump – including one that was produced for his 2024 election campaign. Brennan first reminded Kennedy that in March he had rebuked Kristi Noem, then Trump’s homeland security secretary, for spending millions in government funds “to bolster her public image” in a $220m series of ads she starred in. She then asked the Louisiana senator to comment on the new ads featuring Trump, which the White House calls “public service announcements”. “Our viewers are going to see a 30-second commercial on this program,” Brennan said. “It’s on all major networks – it’s on the cable networks as well. It prominently features President Trump, and there’s a voice praising him as ‘the toughest, most resilient person I ever met’. And at the end, it says ‘paid for by the US government’. Is that the best use of taxpayer money?” Kennedy replied: “Well, first, as to Secretary Noem, what she did was masterclass dumb. She spent $220[m] on commercials about her, and I called her out on it.” “This looks like a commercial about President Trump,” Brennan noted, referring to the first ad in the series, a 30-second highlight reel of Trump’s second presidency, punctuated by on-screen text driving his political agenda and suggesting Democrats are communists. “I don’t think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money … on private ads for themselves,” Kennedy replied. “Now, the White House sees it differently. But … I think there ought to be a rule that you can’t – well, there probably is a rule – you can’t spend public money to promote yourself.” Kennedy, a lawyer with degrees from both the University of Virginia and University of Oxford, appeared to be tacitly acknowledging the argument made by Jamie Raskin, a Democratic congressman and legal scholar, that any government employees who worked on the first pro-Trump ad – “or used government resources to make it” – may have committed a felony violation of the Hatch Act, a law that bars government workers from partisan campaign activities. According to Medium Buying, a company that buys airtime for Republican candidates, the Trump administration used more taxpayer funds to broadcast another partisan ad featuring the president that aired nationwide on Saturday during a college football game between Ohio State and Illinois on Fox. It aired again during Fox News Sunday. That 30-second spot shows a moody, black-and-white shot of Trump staring into the camera as the soundtrack plays the closing riff of a campaign speech he gave dozens of times in 2023 and 2024. “This is the final battle,” Trump says in the ad. “With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state; we will expel the warmongers from our government; we will drive out the globalists; we will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists,” he continues, with cheers from a crowd. Those cheers indicate that the audio was recorded during a campaign rally and at a time before he used his power as president to start a war with Iran that has left some supporters feeling betrayed. “We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate our country from these tyrants and villains once and for all,” Trump can be heard promising in language clearly calculated to appeal to Christian supporters by echoing the biblical story of Jesus driving merchants and money changers from the temple in Jerusalem. The newest ad, with on-screen text reading “Paid for by the US Government”, is even more obviously a partisan product than the first one. In fact, the ad was created for Trump’s 2024 election campaign. And it was posted on his Truth Social account in 2023 and 2024 with a plea for funds from supporters. The rhetoric was written in to Trump’s standard campaign speech as early as July 2023, and then repeated by him again and again at dozens of rallies and appeals for donations. The ad was even played on giant screens during the 2024 Republican national convention before Trump’s speech accepting his party’s nomination. When it was broadcast during the convention by C-Span on 18 July 2024, the ad was identified as material “provided by the Republican National Committee”. At the end of his interview with CBS on Sunday, Kennedy volunteered that he also opposed Trump’s drive to put his own name on public buildings. “I also think that we ought to have a rule that no politician can have a building named after him while he’s alive,” Kennedy said, before adding that there was such a statute in his home state. “Well, we’ll watch, Senator, if you introduce that,” Brennan responded.

webTitle: Blanche defends Trump’s White House media ban: ‘It is a privilege, not a right’

fields.headline: Blanche defends Trump’s White House media ban: ‘It is a privilege, not a right’
fields.trailText: US attorney general argues that president was ‘sick and tired’ of inaccurate reporting by CNN, MS Now and Politico
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump’s attorney general, Todd Blanche, argued on Sunday that the administration was permitted to ban three news outlets from the White House because “it is a privilege and not a right to be there”. Appearing on the ABC News program This Week during the second week of the White House’s dispute over press credentialing and access, Blanche also said that the administration took the decision to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico beginning on 19 September because the president was “sick and tired” of what he considered to be those media outlets’ inaccurate reporting. Blanche offered no evidence for his claim that the outlets’ reporting was inaccurate, rather than simply unflattering to the president. Pressed by the interviewer, Martha Raddatz, to point to a report the administration objected to, Blanche seemed to suggest that any negative reporting about Trump must be inaccurate. “Wait, give you an example of when CNN doesn’t report accurately? You cannot be asking me that,” Blanche replied. “There’s not even a real dispute that the information coming out of CNN and some of these other networks is wholly and completely, almost 100% negative toward the president.” On Thursday, a judge issued a temporary restraining order requiring the White House to temporarily restore the credentials of affected journalists, and they were allowed entry to the executive complex. But on Saturday, CNN said its journalists were barred from joining the press pool traveling with the president on Air Force One. “The president hasn’t denied access,” Blanche told ABC. “That’s not the right way to describe it.” The continuing dispute between the administration and the White House press corps had appeared to be resolving before CNN was again blocked from providing pool TV coverage of Trump on Saturday. That was after outlets stood in solidarity with CNN, MS Now and Politico by briefly refusing to provide any pool TV feeds of the president. On ABC, Blanche said it was not unusual for a news outlet to not be allowed on to the president’s plane. “The White House routinely decides who can go on Air Force One,” Blanche said. “This wasn’t a one-time denial of CNN. There’s all kinds of times when certain reporters are not flying or are flying. “It’s not unusual, and as a matter of fact, it’s common every time the president travels that he and his team decide which reporters get to travel with the president.” What Blanche did not explain is that, before Trump’s second term, the choice of which correspondents were part of the pool covering presidential travel was left to the White House Correspondents’ Association and the broadcast networks that take turns providing camera crews. After Trump returned to office last year, the White House took control of which outlets would be permitted in the Oval Office, or on Air Force One, leading to increased access for partisan, pro-Trump journalists. Blanche repeated the administration’s position that the affected three outlets’ reporting amounted to a “national security problem”. Raddatz reminded Blanche that Trump himself said he had banned CNN, MS Now and Politico, because, he said, “they purposely write negative news, and they do that because they want to diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration”. In the ruling to temporarily restore the three banned outlets’ White House access for 14 days, US district judge Timothy Kelly said there was nothing in the record suggesting that revocation of the press passes was motivated by national security concerns. “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ plaintiffs from the White House – instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly wrote in his ruling. Trump was faced with a gloomy political landscape with just over a month before the federal midterm elections in November. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found Trump’s overall public approval rating to be at 32%, an all-time low. But confidence in the news media polls lower, with just 28% expressing a “great deal” or “fair amount” of trust in newspapers, television channels and radio outlets to report the news fully, accurately and fairly, according to a 2025 Gallup survey. Bill Clinton recently commented on the battle between what the news media see as a crude effort at censorship and a denial of constitutional rights – and what the White House views as unfairly negative reporting. “There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps,” the former president said at the Clinton Global Initiative 2026 summit. “And there’s a reason we have a constitution – because none of us are immune from being pissed off. “But I’m glad I never did, and I’m glad I couldn’t. And these people shouldn’t. The law should be what it is.” Blanche was asked what the US constitution’s first amendment – which guarantees the right to a free press – meant to him. “The law says – what the free press can do is they are free to report whatever they want,” Blanche remarked. “Of course, they can. But when it comes to the White House, it is the people’s house. It is a privilege and not a right to be there.” He added that “it is absolutely the president’s duty to make sure that the American people are hearing accurate news.”

webTitle: UN ambassador Waltz says Iran was not negotiating ‘in good faith’ to end war

fields.headline: UN ambassador Waltz says Iran was not negotiating ‘in good faith’ to end war
fields.trailText: Waltz says Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to end war because they ‘were asking for everything up front’
fields.bodyText: The Trump administration’s ambassador to the United Nations said the US rejected Iran’s proposal to end the ongoing war there because Iranian negotiators “were asking for everything up front”. Echoing comments by Donald Trump on Saturday, the president’s UN ambassador, Mike Waltz, told CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday that Iran had asked for relief “from billions and billions of sanctions that are going into place” as part of an economic blockade on Iran. The blockade is aimed at putting pressure on Iran to stop its attacks ‌on vessels in the strait of Hormuz. “They were asking for everything up front with a promise that they would then talk,” Waltz said on State of the Union. “The president is just not confident that the Iranians are coming in good faith and that we will truly negotiate the end of their nuclear program.” Trump said on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s peace plan, proposed at ⁠the recent UN general assembly in New York, arguing that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway. “They want to make a deal ⁠to open the Hormuz strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump said. Trump said the US was “winning tremendously” and had “total control of the Hormuz strait”. In comments to Axios on Sunday, Trump said he expected more talks with Iran during the upcoming week. “They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make,” the outlet quoted the president as saying. “It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand.” Earlier, Waltz pointed to the failed US-Iran memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in Pakistan in June that laid out a 14-point framework agreement for a negotiated peace. Iran, he said, “immediately violated it by attacking international shipping, in violation of international law, and 146 nations have joined us in condemning Iran for those attacks”. Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the US and Israel. “Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, posted on social media. “Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock.” Araghchi also appeared on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, saying his country was prepared to resume fighting with the US but had not yet abandoned diplomacy after Trump rejected Iran’s peace proposal. “We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed,” Araghchi said. “We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war. “At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose.” The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said his country was ready for talks on its nuclear program and other issues – but would not accept “bullying or coercion”. “Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”. On CNN, Waltz also addressed recent reports that China had assisted Iran in missile targeting of shipping in the strait of Hormuz and on US military bases in the region. Waltz did not confirm the leaked intelligence assessments but said Trump had raised the issue with China’s president, Xi Jinping, during the latter’s recent state visit to the US capital Washington DC. Trump had also done so “multiple times” previously, including during his visit to China in May, according to Waltz. “I think we have seen movement in a positive direction,” Waltz said. “President Trump has made it clear it’s unacceptable.” Waltz pointed to readouts of the high-level meeting that said the US and China had “agreed that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon”. “They cannot and should not be tolling, much less attacking, international shipping in an international waterway,” Waltz said. “So I think that was incredibly important to hear from President Xi coming out of the summit.” Waltz also rejected reporting in the Wall Street Journal that the US would resume bombing Iran after the federal midterm elections in November. He pointed to Trump’s comments that Iran was miscalculating. “The president is looking to make not just this generation – but the next generation – safer by not allowing what is essentially a terrorist organization in [Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] that is controlling the levers of government and wants to march towards a nuclear weapon,” Waltz said. “We’re not going to let the IRGC have a nuclear weapon, much less hold the world hostage with one.”

webTitle: Saturday Night Live: Jalen Brunson makes for stiff host in underwhelming season premiere

fields.headline: Saturday Night Live: Jalen Brunson makes for stiff host in underwhelming season premiere
fields.trailText: There are some promising moments from newer cast members, but the show’s return, after a politically tumultuous period, was lacking in bite
fields.bodyText: The 52nd season of Saturday Night Live opens inside the New York City mayor’s office. Mayor Zohran Mamdani (Ramy Youssef, reprising the role from last season) gets a surprise visit from Donald Trump (James Austin Johnson). The president, who “for some reason that no one can figure out” loves Mamdani, has braved the big El Niño storm to visit his “day one”. Trump unloads about his busy week – banning members of the press from the White House pool, delivering apocalyptic threats to Iran at the UN, consulting with AI leaders including Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg (“It made me think, wow, RFK Jr’s probably right about those vaccines, I mean, the ‘tizz in that room …”) – before being interrupted by his assistant Natalie Harp (Ashley Padilla). Acting like “the girl from Obsession, but blond”, the dangerously jealous Harp threatens Mamdani. Trump eventually convinces the mayor to let him stay and hang out in New York in exchange for $20bn for a housing project in Queens. A rather weak cold open considering it’s the season premiere. Padilla’s caricature of Harp as a deranged, Fatal Attraction-like stalker is gold and should have been the focus here. Unfortunately, the show decided to lean on Mamdani, which might have worked if they got someone else to portray him, preferably a cast member – you’d think they’d want to bring in someone who could play that role given how prominent a national figure he’s become – or, failing that, a guest with more star wattage than Youssef. Jalen Brunson, the basketball champion and conquering hero of the Big Apple, hosts for the first time. The MVP point guard stumbles over his first lines, which is appropriate considering he promises to approach the episode like he would a Knicks Finals game: “The first three quarters of the show are gonna be godawful, but the last sketch is gonna be amazing.” He teases a musical performance before discarding the idea, briefly brings out his hater Stephen A Smith (Kenan Thompson) to apologize, and fields some questions and ribbing from four of his teammates in the audience. Brunson’s stoicism can definitely be used for deadpan laughs, but watching the goofily charismatic Karl-Anthony Towns here, one can’t help but think he may have been the better choice to host. A post-lunch work meeting gets sidetracked by a game of wastebasket hoops, as Brunson’s office drone, Darius, misses a couple of easy shots and keeps putting time back on an imaginary clock to try to sink one. He scores the biggest laugh of the night early, responding to the lone female co-worker (Sarah Sherman) patronizingly telling him he’s out of food wrappers with “Am I, bitch?” before pulling out a basket stuffed with them. A new season of Dream Academy searches for a new breakout girl group. However, contestants find themselves saddled with two hopeless hot messes: Duff (Jane Wickline) and Margle (Grace Reiter), who only got on the show because they witnessed the executive producer commit a hit-and-run. Despite being completely ill-suited to pop stardom, they manage to win the competition with their bizarre single Newton’s Cradle. Season one winners (and tonight’s music guests), Katseye, show up to introduce their new music video. This makes for a good showcase for Wickline, recently promoted to the main cast, and brand-new featured player Reiter. The latter, who has a ready-made fanbase thanks to her prominence on YouTube and TikTok, debuts to a noticeably loud round of applause. What we first assume is a meeting of Alcoholics Anonymous is revealed to be a support group for men whose wives and girlfriends were brought on stage at an Usher-Chris Brown concert. The men all talk about the trauma of having their ladies dry-humped and seduced on stage and across social media. The best line comes via Kam Patterson, who ruefully asks: “If God is real, why would he create talented light-skins?” High School Musical: The New Generation sees Brunson play a transfer student who tries out for the North High basketball team, brutally dominating and humiliating the Zac Efron-like captain during his big musical number. The punishment doesn’t stop on the court, as he easily seduces the kid’s girlfriend. Short and mean, it makes good use of Brunson’s icy demeanor and Jeremy Culhane’s theater kid energy. During a long layover, two businessmen (Mikey Day and Brunson) relieve their stress by using the business-class air-massage chairs. They enjoy them a little too loudly, making the other passengers deeply uncomfortable with their orgasmic moaning and writhing. This is pretty much a one-man show for Day, who is always best when cut loose from his usual straight-man roles. On Weekend Update, returning anchors Colin Jost and Michael Che cover the week’s news stories, including Benjamin Netanyahu addressing an empty chamber at the UN following a walkout of delegates protesting against his country’s war on Gaza. Per Che: “I guess wherever Netanyahu shows up, there’s gonna be some relocating.” Che circles back to this topic a little later, reporting that Macklemore, the rapper who was dropped as the opening act for Ed Sheeran over his public support of Gaza, plans to stage his own Free Palestine tour. The live audience cheers, before Che asks: “But haven’t the Palestinian people been through enough?” Update’s first guest is Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei (Wickline, sporting some bang-on prosthetics). After recently sounding the alarm over the existential threat to humanity posed by AI, Amodei exclaims: “If we can pressure lawmakers to create guardrails, we will be able to stop me.” Mumbling and dissociating like Gollum from Lord of the Rings, he attempts to reassure everyone that AI won’t kill us all, but utterly fails by blurting out the truth: “AI is the devil, and I its maker!” Later, Jost invites the political pundit Tucker Carlson on to discuss this summer’s hit movies, such as The Odyssey (“It’s so nice to see Greek people do something other than make women feel uncomfortable”), Spider-Man (“Brand New Gender”), Obsession (“The left’s idea of a horror movie is that a woman is forced to love a man”), and Minions and Monsters (“I’m not talking about the children’s film, I’m talking about the Trump cabinet”). Culhane’s Carlson impersonation, which has been a big hit on social media, is very convincing on a surface level, but the caricaturization remains years out of date, although at least they’ve finally acknowledged that Carlson has become critical of Trump. But that’s not enough, and so long as Culhane and co continue to present Carlson as an old-school Christian neocon, as opposed to the anti-interventionist (and particularly anti-Israel) hardliner and ultra-white nationalist that he is today, it will remain blunted. The next sketch sees a third-grade teacher (Ben Marshall) meet with the mother of one of his gifted students, as well as her numerous lovers. It’s a flimsy setup seemingly developed around the closing line: “Let’s just say, I’m always late for the bus, but I’m never late for the train.” Then, two self-described feminist inventors (Marshall and Culhane) present their creation – a pair of eyeglasses that loudly beep when the wearer stares at a woman’s breasts – on Shark Tank. They can’t make it more than a couple of seconds before their invention goes wild any time there’s a woman nearby. In the closing sketch, Brunson, playing himself, finds himself harassed by a pair of scammers claiming to be his old third-grade coach and father, respectively. A risque joke involving someone giving oral sex to Spider-Man gets a big guffaw, but otherwise, this is a weak note to end on. Brunson made for an expectedly stiff host, but he was by no means terrible. As far as pro athletes who have hosted over the last few seasons, he ranks somewhere in the middle. The bigger issue was the overall lack of excitement. Outside a few moments where the newly elevated or freshman cast members got to shine, this felt more like a mid-season episode rather than a season premiere – especially one that lands just a little more than a month out from midterm elections. Hopefully SNL has more exciting and politically relevant material in store for the next few weeks.

webTitle: What Democrats are getting right – and wrong – in run-up to midterms: ‘We can’t just be anti-Trump’

fields.headline: What Democrats are getting right – and wrong – in run-up to midterms: ‘We can’t just be anti-Trump’
fields.trailText: Grassroots organizer Yasmin Radjy on the Democratic ground game leading into the midterm elections
fields.bodyText: In the run-up to the US midterm elections, Swing Left – a grassroots political group focused on electing Democrats to office – has spent time canvassing in dozens of districts across the country to hear from hundreds of thousands of voters. Now, with fewer than 40 days until the US midterm elections, the group’s executive director, Yasmin Radjy, sets out what she feels Democrats have been getting right and wrong this election cycle, and why these races are vital for the party’s future control of the US Congress in the years to come. We are now five weeks out. What do you feel have been, and will continue to be, the defining issues of these midterm races? Yasmin Radjy: The two things head and shoulders above everything else that we’re hearing about: one is a feeling like the system is broken, and soon after that are various issues around cost of living. The two are often related, but there are very few conversations where one or both of those issues are not coming up. Everyone’s gotten the memo that we need to talk about affordability. I don’t think there’s a Republican or a Democrat who’s not aware of that. The candidates who are really standing out this cycle again across the ideological spectrum, from Abdul El-Sayed [in Michigan] to Mary Peltola [in Alaska]. And on the House map, Paige Cognetti [in Pennsylvania], to Amish Shah [in Arizona]. They are connecting those dots in a way that is specific and that is also mirroring the nature of those districts. What do you think the party needs to focus on to regain trust, and establish a clear sense of identity with voters moving forward – particularly after 2024? We have to follow up with people when they express urgency around the very real and material concerns that they have. When they express disappointment, we can’t pretend like everything is going great. We also need to acknowledge that a lot of the things we’ve been doing aren’t working. That requires having tough, not just conversations, but introspection, and openness to trying new things, testing new things and taking bigger, riskier swings than we’re accustomed to. On one of the must-win races you mentioned – the open Senate seat in Michigan – what do you feel voters are responding to with a candidate like Abdul El-Sayed? What do you think he needs to do in order to win over voters in that state that Trump won? I think something he is modeling is a “talk to everybody and engage with everyone” approach, not just talk to the people who already agree with you. I think he really won his primary because of organizing. In terms of the issues and themes in Michigan, what we’re hearing is very similar to elsewhere with subtle differences: both parties suck, and no politician cares about that voter, their community and people like them. That is ubiquitous. What he is able to speak compellingly on with a lot of authority is his feeling like the system is broken, and he is doing a good job of tying that to affordability and a whole host of other issues. I’m curious what you think might be the biggest obstacle for Democrats in this cycle? What could be getting in the party’s way? One is that we continue to not have a sufficiently clear answer, for a time when the winds are not blowing in our direction, of what Democrats stand for besides being anti-Trump. We need to start answering that now – and it’s OK if that answer has shades of difference in Michigan, Alaska and North Carolina. The second piece is we cannot assume our base will be with us again because of anti-Trump sentiment in a way that can sustain durable power. Something under-discussed that keeps me up at night is if we are not building long-term, durable power, by 2030 we are going to wake up to an election where, if we don’t have power in the states, we will not be able to win congressional majorities because of how bad redistricting will look. Population shifts are clear in California and New York – two big blue states essential for presidential math – and they will be losing electoral college votes starting in 2030. Texas and Florida are the inverse – they are going to gain power. If we don’t treat the midterms as our most important moment to build infrastructure while there’s money pouring in, while there’s energy to have a shot at winning tough Republican seats in a way we can sustain, we are going to lose without question in the future, because we will have squandered an opportunity. I want to discuss the concerns about progressives, from establishment Democrats. What’s your response to those in the coalition who question whether these progressive candidates have a real shot in battlegrounds that the party wants to either retain or flip? We have members who are Democratic Socialists of America members. We have members who think DSA is a huge threat to democracy – we’ve got the full gamut. Our perspective is that the fixation on ideology and the DSA-versus-centrist divide is a completely false binary. We need to win a majority, and there is a level of pragmatism among the grassroots that is underappreciated. The binary will crumble, not because it doesn’t exist in our institutions, but because that’s not how voters are. We talk to voters every day who might be DSA-aligned on healthcare and Blue Dog-aligned on the border, and it’s the same person. If we lead with genuine curiosity and openness to listening to voters, we immediately see that voters are idiosyncratic, strange and full of contradictions because they’re human. Linked to this, I’m thinking about James Talarico [the Democratic nominee for the US Senate seat in Texas] and Rob Sand [the Democratic gubernatorial nominee in Iowa]. They are showing a pivot in their messaging, particularly when it comes to trans rights. Do you feel that is a necessary strategy right now to court those swing voters, independents and moderates in newly competitive battleground states? I think when you go out and really talk to people, specifically on the issue of trans rights, most Americans want trans people to have rights – and the areas of discomfort range from lack of knowledge. Their worldview on trans issues is curated by Fox News, so there is an information gap. Most voters, including many Democrats, have complicated feelings about the trans people in sports issue. The answer is not to start repeating Fox News talking points. The way to talk about these issues – and this is what the data shows – is to break down the pieces: all Americans want every American to have a certain set of freedoms. The trans and sports issue is complicated, and it is not really a decision for governments, it’s a decision for the leagues. I think Sarah McBride is a perfect example of this – leading with grace, recognizing that changing hearts and minds takes time, and that people use clunky language along the way. Looking ahead, do you think Democrats are doing enough to respond to Donald Trump’s efforts to undermine elections in this cycle in particular? I would say there is an asymmetric investment in election protection right now. And that asymmetric investment is on the litigation front, it is on the donor-organizing and on the grassroots-organizing fronts. And I feel really confident and really relieved, candidly, that the amount of investment of time, talent and strategy has been placed on that. The flip side is the progressive ecosystem, overall, has not invested as much in the actual act of winning the election, and there is nothing more important for election protection than winning each competitive race by a big enough margin that Trump doesn’t have the incentive to try any kind of funny business. We are not where we should be in some of the most competitive races in the country in terms of dollars invested and volunteers ready to help that candidate, and to me, that is the most essential ingredient to election protection. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

webTitle: Bad language: profane Trump brings presidential swearing out into open

fields.headline: Bad language: profane Trump brings presidential swearing out into open
fields.trailText: President has let rip with swearwords in recent months, redefining norms about acceptable language in public office
fields.bodyText: With a lifetime of political memories stretching back to John F Kennedy’s assassination and the Black civil rights struggles of the 1960s, Cheryl Johnson had one complaint above all else about today’s politicians: the swearing. “All this cursing in politics, we never heard that before,” said Johnson, a retired social worker living in the Pittsburgh area. “Words are very powerful, and the past 45 presidents of this country, have not used such vile language. “Is that how teachers, corporate leaders, nurses, doctor, dentist speak in their work environment? It’s not OK. It’s a decline in respect and honor, period.” Over the past decade, Donald Trump has been at the vanguard of redefining public standards of what constitutes acceptable language. Having already been criticized for debasing and coarsening the public discourse during his first presidency – when he was memorably reported to have complained that US was admitting immigrants from “shithole countries” – Trump has let rip during his second. He has repeatedly used, and seemingly normalized, words never previously heard in public from a US president, at least not intentionally. A taboo seemed to be broken in June 2025, when Trump profanely condemned Israel and Iran for continuing firing at each other even after hostilities were thought to have been halted following a 12-day war. “They don’t know what they fuck they’re doing,” he told reporters on the White House lawn. Lest that should be taken as slip of the tongue, Trump indulged his growing taste for public obscenity again in October 2025, when asked about Venezuela’s then president, Nicolas Maduro. “He’s offered everything,” claimed Trump. “You know why? Because he doesn’t want to fuck around with the United States.” (Months later, Maduro was seized by US special forces. He is now in custody in New York, awaiting trial.) Trump has used profanity even more starkly in recent social media posts, deploying it to raise rhetorical pressure on Tehran after it closed the strait of Hormuz following Trump’s decision to launch the US-Israel war on Iran in February. “Open the Fuckin’ Strait, you crazy bastards, or you’ll be living in Hell - JUST WATCH,” he posted on his Truth Social platform in April. “President Trump doesn’t have a very strong sense of decorum,” said Michael Adams, a professor of English language at Indiana University Bloomington, and author of In Praise of Profanity, a study of swearing’s place in society. “The swearing has a whole range of aspects to it. Some of it is this emphatic diplomatic persona, and some of it is believing in the unpredictability of the president, and his general sense that he doesn’t care.” Civility in politics Trump is hardly the first president with a taste for the profane. Lyndon Johnson and Richard Nixon were both renowned for liberal use of earthy vernacular, but in private. Their bad language was only exposed when tape recordings of their conversations were released after their presidencies. In Nixon’s case, his swearing became an issue during Watergate, when the White House released heavily-redacted transcripts of his taped conversations – with repeated use of the telling phrase “expletive deleted”. Trump’s increasingly cavalier approach to obscenity is a far cry from George W Bush’s mortified response when he was a US presidential candidate in September 2000. During the campaign, a live mic picked up his description of a New York Times journalist as a “major-league asshole”. A chastened Bush, running on a pledge to restore civility to politics, voiced “regret” that his remark was heard. These days, by contrast, politicians are only too keen for voters to hear what would once have been indiscretions, according to analysts. While Trump may have opened the floodgates, other officials and candidates – Republican and Democrat alike – have followed through. Joseph Phillips, an American politics professor at Trinity College Dublin, puts this down to a search for authenticity in an era when politicians have fallen in public esteem. “The incentive for politicians to use profanity [comes from] a change in how people view the profession,” Phillips said. “The level of political trust that Americans have has declined a lot, and this has changed how people see politicians. “Politicians have the incentive to buck that particular trend of appearing unscrupulous and unrelatable by doing a very cheap thing that we all can do, which is using language more typical of ordinary people, which would include cursing.” In that vein, US vice-president JD Vance has commonly used the word “shit”, in speeches and on social media, to bait political opponents and critics. Speaking at a military base in Kentucky on Thanksgiving last year, Vance drew criticism after telling soldiers who raised their hands when asked if they liked eating turkey that they were “full of shit”. Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, has used scatalogical terms to deride previous practices in the armed forces he regards as woke, telling a gathering of generals at a marine base in Quantico, Virginia last September: “We’re done with that shit.” Democrats, too, have embraced verbal vulgarity. Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey told Immigration Customs and Enforcement (ICE) agents to “get the fuck out” of the city after an agent shot dead a mother-of-three, Renee Nicole Good, in her vehicle in January. Earlier this week Tammy Duckworth, a Democratic senator from Illinois, told a Washington thinktank she was “tired of fixing shit that Republicans break”. Arguing against being polite if the Democrats regain control of the Senate in November’s midterm elections, she said: “Fuck that shit.” A rhetorical maneuver While the long-term impact may be to reduce public respect for politics even further, those competing for office are unlikely to care. “The incentive of an individual politician is probably not to regain the esteem of the profession, but instead to ensure their own election or re-election,” argued Phillips. “It wouldn’t be the first time that politicians have run sacrificing a broader institution for personal gain.” Adams, of Indiana University, said politicians were seeking “covert prestige” in descending into coarse language. “There is a covert prestige to swearing that has to do with the swashbuckling image of the inveterate swearer – a sort of devil-may-care attitude that attracts people,” he said. “People do swear, and if you never swear, then people wonder if you’re really like them enough that you would be a good president for them. “It’s comparable to when George W Bush and Barack Obama were campaigning and people asked: ‘Would you want to have a beer with them?’ It wasn’t a glass of vintage wine, or a very old single malt – it was a plebeian drink with the plebs. Swearing fits into the same rhetorical maneuver.” Benjamin Bergen, a professor of cognitive science at the University of California, San Diego, and author of “WHAT THE F: What Swearing Reveals About Our Language, Our Brains, and Ourselves,” suggested the heated language was being fueled by the fact that “we are in a very strident time of political disagreement”. The polarized atmosphere, he said, could mean it is only a matter of time before previously unthinkable – let alone utterable – profanities crop up in presidential inaugural speeches, or State of the Union addresses. “I don’t see any reason why there’s anything special about a State of the Union address or a speech in front of the UN, or anything like that,” said Bergen. “I think the language norms are just changing.” But the pendulum could eventually swing back from the current profane trends, he suggested. “If politicians of one generation are seen to be swearing all the time, the next generation may just reject that entirely.” In a curious transatlantic distinction, Phillips – who previously worked in the UK – said the US tendency towards swearing has yet to be replicated in British and Irish politics. “We’re dealing with similar loss of political trust in all three countries,” he said. “However, there is one way in which the US differs, and that’s in the incentives for politicians to build personal brands. “Politicians’ fates in the UK and Ireland are much more tied to the fate of the party. So the incentive to change an established mode of behavior just isn’t quite as high.”

webTitle: Burnham’s plan for a radical reset collides with economic reality | Heather Stewart

fields.headline: Burnham’s plan for a radical reset collides with economic reality
fields.trailText: Surging energy bills, higher borrowing costs and rising inflation have left the PM and his chancellor in a fiscal bind
fields.bodyText: As Labour heads to Liverpool this week, Andy Burnham has promised to deliver “stability” in the public finances; but the economic backdrop is anything but stable. The longer the US-Israeli war on Iran persists, the more likely it is that UK consumers will have to swallow higher mortgage rates and energy bills – just as the government is wrestling with its own surging borrowing costs. We are only a few weeks into the three-month period tracking energy price moves that the regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem, will use as a basis to set the energy price cap in January – but it’s been a pretty bleak period so far, with the cost of a barrel of crude above $100 for much of that time. Based on the pricing in energy futures markets, the Bank of England reckons Ofgem could increase the energy price cap, which sets the maximum energy rates paid by homes on standard tariffs, by an eye-watering 24% in January. At the same time, the Bank’s policymakers – from the governor, Andrew Bailey, down – have repeatedly signalled that while they are reassured high energy prices have not yet fed through into wider inflation, they can’t hold off from raising rates for much longer. “We’ve made it quite clear … that it’s going to be harder to maintain that stance, the longer we have high energy prices,” Andrew Bailey said on Friday. Or as his deputy, Sarah Breeden, who like Bailey did not vote to raise rates in September, put it: “The more sparks we’re throwing in the tinderbox, the more likely we might have to turn the hose on it.” Donald Trump made clear over the weekend that he has no intention of staunching the flames himself, by bringing the conflict to a close. “I’m rejecting their deal,” he told reporters, after Iran made a fresh proposal. “They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly … we’re winning tremendously.” With UK inflation already above 3% and likely to rise further, markets are expecting the Bank to raise rates four times, to 4.75%, over the next 12 months. Such a situation almost certainly won’t happen – the economy would probably be clobbered into submission long before they got there, and inflation with it. But Bailey and his colleagues are widely expected to make a start in November, the week after John Healey’s first budget. Policymakers will also have to reckon with the impact on prices of what is expected to be the most powerful El Niño weather system in 1,000 years, which as well as being devastating to human life, is likely to drive up the cost of important foodstuffs. Burnham has made offering the public a “breathing space” from higher costs a hallmark of his early weeks in power, with sensible but modest policies, such as the £2 bus fare cap. A new iteration of the Tories’ help-to-buy scheme for first-time homebuyers will follow at the budget, he announced this weekend. But while these offerings show a government keen to help, they risk being overshadowed by the wider picture. With the threat of a surge in energy bills looming, the government is keen to avoid announcing a large new support package, conscious of the cumulative cost of Labour’s interventions over the last year. “I think people need to remember that measures have already been taken,” Burnham said this weekend. These include the £2.3bn Rachel Reeves spent on lowering energy bills – including by shifting some green levies on to general taxation – and his own VAT cut on domestic electricity, which the Treasury has yet to explain how it will fund. Yet if, as Trump has hinted, the conflict continues until after the midterm elections in early November, global oil and gas prices could remain high for many more weeks – locking in a sharp rise in bills for UK consumers in the new year. Economists are urging Healey to be bold on energy in the budget, rather than wait and hope. Experts at the research and innovation foundation Nesta are calling for a gas price stabiliser, for example, that would cushion the blow of higher prices now, at the Treasury’s expense – but bring in additional revenue as market prices dropped in future. Any policy that cuts utility bills has the added bonus of bearing down on inflation, helping ease the pressure on the Bank to act. Adding to Labour’s woes, though, the government’s cost of borrowing has risen sharply in recent weeks, alongside that of other big economies, as the global bond selloff has gathered pace. It has been yet another harsh reminder of how exposed the government’s fiscal position is to the vagaries of global markets, with a knock-on effect for the budget forecasts. There are growing warnings, too, about the risks of market instability caused by the interaction of febrile bond markets and the AI mega-bubble. Labour was already in a tricky fiscal bind, given demands for higher defence spending – not least from Healey himself, who now has the job of finding the resources. The difficult decisions about how to do so – let alone fund Burnham’s wider priorities – look likely to be delayed until a spending review some time in 2027. It is very hard to see how that won’t necessitate a fresh round of tax rises. The plan had been for a relatively modest budget, focusing on plans for devolution, and filling the gaps in the defence investment plan announced in the summer. This caution looked out of step with Burnham’s promise of a radical political reset and may be untenable if energy bills are going to soar. He and Healey face a tough autumn.

webTitle: Trump allies could use midterms ‘counting window’ to disrupt results, experts warn

fields.headline: Trump allies could use midterms ‘counting window’ to disrupt results, experts warn
fields.trailText: Fears grow that loyalists in key states could use critical period when votes are counted to amplify false claims
fields.bodyText: Election experts have warned Donald Trump’s administration could use the crucial hours and days after November’s midterm elections to disrupt the results after struggling to enforce a crackdown on voting. With less than six weeks remaining until polls close, and control of US Congress in the balance, the post-election “counting window” is seen as as a particularly vulnerable moment by former US federal government officials. While the US president’s bid to impose sweeping restrictions on mail-in ballots was rejected by the supreme court earlier this month, there is apprehension that Trump and his allies could use the period while votes are counted to amplify unfounded allegations in a bid to challenge results that don’t go their way. “I think because the administration has lost so many of their attempts to disrupt the normal process in court, that they are going to use the claim of foreign interference at the end of voting days to either seize equipment or to seize ballots, whether they’re legally justified to do so or not,” Caitlin Durkovich, a former deputy homeland security adviser for resilience and response on the national security council, told a briefing staged by the Brennan Center for Justice earlier this week. Some states take days – even weeks, in California’s case – to complete a count of votes after an election. Control of the House of Representatives and Senate may hinge on results in states with a delayed result. “That period, that waiting time, is where doubt begins to surface,” Durkovich said on Tuesday. “And when it is then amplified by foreign actors and, frankly, by domestic actors, it starts to cause distrust in the integrity of the process.” State-level elections officials are trying to prepare the public to understand the process now, to head off a manufactured controversy later, said Larry Norden, vice-president of the elections and government program at the Brennan Center. “To me, this is the biggest threat right now,” he said. “I think a lot of people may think just because they’re seeing all these headlines being thrown at them that things have changed – that it’s become more difficult to vote,” added Norden. “In the history of American elections in some ways, there have never been more options for the way that people can vote, and they are still in place going into this election.” Early voting eliminates most of the threats voters apprehend ahead of an election, he suggested. “The earlier they vote, the more secure they can feel that their vote is going to count, and I think that’s a really important message for us to be delivering to people.” The power of doubt about the validity of votes, and the risk of Trump unveiling “emergency” measures on ballots or voting machines around election day, looms large. “Every state in the country now has live ballots out,” said Ben Hovland, former chair of the Election Assistance Commission. “That really means the election is here, and it means that needs to be taken into consideration for any court rulings we’re looking at.” A supreme court decision this month upheld a lower-court injunction on the Trump administration using the US Postal Service and the Department of Homeland Security to vet mail-in ballot deliveries. But groups such as the NAACP, the National Urban League and other rights organizations remain concerned about the Trump administration’s insistent claim – without evidence – that the 2026 midterm elections will be illegitimate unless the federal government intervenes. Normally, the Department of Justice and the FBI enter a “quiet period” just ahead of elections, to avoid influencing the results. That has not been the case this year. The Department of Homeland Security continues to pursue voter-roll lists in states that would not turn them over voluntarily. The federal government has asked states to retain their 2024 election documentation for later inquiries. And DHS is pursuing an independent “unlawful voter initiative” to find non-citizen voters on state rolls, one that an anonymous whistleblower told congress last week that is using “highly questionable data” and may be unlawful. The federal government’s claims of illegally-registered voters – claiming numbers that do not bear up under scrutiny – and Trump’s rhetoric alleging fraud without evidence, “back up a narrative of fraud to undermine confidence in the elections”, Hovland said. Much of the president’s election rhetoric revolves around foreign interference. Experts make a distinction between foreign influence – propaganda, essentially – and foreign interference , or directly manipulating vote counts. “It’s very important for people to understand that we don’t have any examples of a country trying to interfere in the electoral process, in that technical process,” said Beth Sanner, a former deputy director of national intelligence who is now director for geopolitics and strategy at International Capital Strategies. “It just didn’t happen,” she said. “It didn’t happen in 2020.” Election security has improved across the country, partially as a reaction to false claims about Trump’s 2020 defeat. “Every state audits its results,” said Geoff Hales, former chief of joint cyber defense collaborative partnerships at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA. “Election officials across the country have really taken cybersecurity seriously.” Despite the president’s insistence that the country faces a foreign threat to elections, Hale said the federal government has sharply cut staff and spending on elections security at CISA, and with it the technical assistance that once flowed to state election’s officers. “The federal support that used to be there has pulled back sharply,” he added. “This means that cybersecurity services have been reduced, funding for information sharing environments have been cut, the threat briefings about nation-state adversaries that used to occur dozens of times a year are occurring rarely or not at all.”

webTitle: Most Americans don’t know Hasan Piker. The rest say he is changing this year’s elections

fields.headline: Most Americans don’t know Hasan Piker. The rest say he is changing this year’s elections
fields.trailText: The popular Twitch streamer has been vilified by Republicans, but the socialist commentator has a large audience that some Democrats have courted
fields.bodyText: It’s only 9am and the latest media shitstorm is well under way. Hasan Piker scrolls through his social media feeds as he comes down the stairs of his home in West Hollywood. An interview with Axios, in which Piker said the US had committed more atrocities than al-Qaida, is blowing up his phone. Requests from reporters are streaming in. Comments on the interview flood his replies. Just another day, and just another news cycle, for a 35-year-old socialist streamer who has no elected or appointed power. Never mind that many voters don’t know who Piker is – and haven’t heard of Twitch, his streaming platform of choice – despite months of concerted efforts by political opponents to elevate his profile, and tie Democratic candidates to his most incendiary comments. Facing an uphill battle to retain control of Congress in November’s US midterm elections, and struggling to land on a coherent message to rally support, Republicans have fixated on Piker – and held him up as a representative of their political targets, from socialists and leftists to Muslims. Voters, so far, don’t seem to care about Piker – at least not more than the cost of gas, or the war in Iran, or healthcare, or artificial intelligence, or immigration, or corruption. Around the country, many told the Guardian they hadn’t heard of Piker, or they knew who he was and sometimes had opinions, but those opinions didn’t factor into their voting decisions. Still, Piker features in Republican campaign ads. A photo of him nearly nude, inexplicably, appeared on the jumbotron at the party’s midterm convention. And Republicans have tried hard to tie Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in the critical swing state of Michigan, to Piker after El-Sayed campaigned with him in the primary. (The candidate has since distanced himself from Piker.) Fielding questions in quick pockets of time around his hours of streaming, podcasts and media appearances, Piker says he is not overly troubled by such attacks. “Republicans believe this is an incredible narrative, for the record,” he says. “They truly believe that this is successful. I’m willing to bet it’s because they’re fucking brain-poisoned by the internet.” But the spotlight is glaringly bright. He was even called out from the stage of this week’s United Nations general assembly, as the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, singled out one of Piker’s most controversial remarks. Moderate Democrats have also used Piker as a proxy in their battle against their party’s ascendant left, which notched key upsets in primaries this year, challenging the centrist establishment. And Piker won’t shut up. He streams for seven hours nonstop each day, with hundreds of thousands of followers tuning in each hour. And even then, he’s not done. Depicted on the right as an extremist, Piker is trying to be tame, he says. “For the election season, I have tried to be as serious as possible,” he says in his signature suit and tie. Unlike the Democratic primaries, where he appeared alongside his chosen candidates from El-Sayed in Michigan to Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, Piker isn’t campaigning for anyone in the general election. It has not escaped Piker’s notice that Republicans continue to target Democrats over their ties with him, and his more controversial statements. “It’s not necessarily my affiliation that’s so negative,” he suggests. But more questions about him mean fewer questions about policy and their opponents. It’s a missed opportunity when they constantly have to answer “What about Hasan Piker?” Piker says. News cycles focused on Piker are driven by a push to attack progressive candidates, according to him, while news outlets carry negative stories about him in an effort to chase clicks and protect their own relevance in the media ecosystem. But in the longer term, Piker also sees the focus on him as a wider test, for a potential 2028 presidential run from the left by candidate like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the progressive congresswoman. “Most people on the left are in some way, shape or form connected back to my community, or myself, or organizations that I work with,” he says. “This is an active way to try and eliminate a political opponent before it becomes too big of a problem for them.” Who is this guy? Piker was born in New Jersey and grew up mostly in Turkey; his parents – his father a political scientist and his mother an architectural and art historian – are Turkish immigrants. While a student at Rutgers University in New Jersey, he got his start as an intern at the progressive outlet The Young Turks, which was co-founded by his uncle, Cenk Uygur. He went on to host a show on the network and started streaming on Twitch in 2018, eventually leaving The Young Turks to focus on his own platform. He now has more than 3 million followers on Twitch, nearly 2 million on YouTube and nearly 2 million on X. From the start, he made controversial comments – comments that now appear in political ads attacking candidates that Piker has supported. Perhaps the most notable, when in 2019 he said “America deserved 9/11,” features prominently in an ad by Mike Rogers, the Republican contender for US Senate in Michigan, to attack El-Sayed. (Piker has since said the comment was “inappropriate”.) A stream in August led to another round of condemnations. Piker, a frequent critic of Israel, said while talking about the Democratic Michigan congressional candidate Jeremy Moss: “If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone’s going to come around and take action – not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews.” His anti-Israel views, in particular, took center stage in the Michigan Senate primary, where El-Sayed faced the pro-Israel congresswoman Haley Stevens. El-Sayed has worked since his primary win to bring in Jewish voters in the state. In the Axios interview that sparked the shitstorm earlier this month, Piker was asked whether he thought America was worse than al-Qaida, the terrorist group. “Pound for pound, as far as the number of deaths, yes,” he responded. “We have caused tremendous terror all around the world.” Earlier this year, the UK would not allow Piker or Uygur to enter the country to do speaking events, with the Home Office saying their visit “may not be conducive to the public good”. And in Australia in August, a program on the ABC that featured an interview with Piker led to a round of complaints to the national broadcaster. Trump this month called Piker a “terrible liability” who has “a power over some of these Democrats”. The Democratic National Committee chair, Ken Martin, said some of Piker’s comments were “absolutely disgusting and deplorable” and that he “does not represent the Democratic party” or its candidates. After 13 years on camera, Piker concedes that his sheer volume of talking means he is not always considered in his comments. After some 22,000 hours of extemporaneous commentary on hot-button issues, some of his remarks almost inevitably test what people find acceptable. His stream, he notes, is not prepackaged or scripted like the conventional programs of other political commentators. His audience is dedicated, albeit niche. Members of Congress have appeared on his streams, including Ocasio-Cortez in 2020. In 2025, he stepped more into campaigning for democratic socialist and progressive candidates, first with the then future New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani. In the 2026 cycle, he lent his name recognition to El-Sayed, Pennsylvania congressional candidate Rabb, Colorado’s Milat Kiros, Adam Hamawy in New Jersey and others. After Democrats lost the presidential race in 2024, their soul-searching included a quest for a “Joe Rogan of the left” who could counter the influence the right had on podcasts. Rogan, for what it’s worth, has more than 21 million followers on YouTube alone. This elevated Piker’s profile further, but misunderstood the realm of nonstop speaking to camera online. It is inherently not polished, and the potential for controversy exceeds the tolerance of most Democratic politicians. Piker has said that he isn’t the Joe Rogan of the left, that really there could be no such thing. Democrats were looking for someone with a platform like Rogan’s that would be a “lackey for the party”. “I’m not that person,” he says. He could elect to not answer a question posed like the al-Qaida one. He could soft-pedal or redirect or say something he doesn’t really believe. But instead, he takes the opportunity to be in front of larger audiences as a chance to find other people who will resonate with what he’s saying, even if it’s “intentionally provocative”. Candidates reached out to him, he says. It hasn’t brought him more money but has increased viewership on YouTube. If he were truly irrelevant, no candidate would risk associating with him, he says. They had made a calculation – and sometimes campaigns were open with him about that, saying they had tested him in their districts to see if he will help or hurt, he says. “This is bad content. It sucks to admit,” he says. “From my perspective, it’s much easier for me to stay the hell away from real campaigns, and I think part of the reason for why I’m getting attacked so much is so that that is what I do, I sit it out next time, or it’s a lesson for even progressive candidates that they shy away from entertaining my platform at all.” Voters don’t care For voters, Piker is mostly a distraction. “I kind of liken it to following Kim Kardashian,” Phil Verges, a farmer in Spring Valley, Wisconsin, said of Piker. “Now, I don’t – excuse my language – I don’t give a shit.” Verges, who votes mostly for Democrats, said he only started to hear Piker’s name while following El-Sayed’s campaign. The stream is “totally meaningless to me”, he added, “as Joe Rogan is to me”. Two things can be true at once. Piker has sway over a set of dedicated leftwing, often younger, people who can help increase a candidate’s profile in a Democratic primary. But many Americans do not care, or even know, about him. Despite the countless news cycles, a New York Times/Siena poll from mid-September found 62% of likely voters across three US Senate battleground states did not know who Piker was. Even in Michigan, where ads are running about Piker, 54% of voters didn’t know him. Guardian reporters who approached voters across the country encountered the same reality. Some said his name sounded familiar, or that they had only heard it in recent weeks in the media. Rabb, the Democratic congressional candidate in Pennsylvania’s solidly blue third congressional district, was the oldest candidate, at 56, in a crowded primary this year. He credits Piker with having brought awareness to his campaign among a demographic that would have otherwise been hard, and expensive, to reach. Whether Piker’s support won him the primary is “unknowable”, Rabb said, but it “significantly increased” his capacity to reach more people – and bring on more volunteers to talk about his candidacy. “What he could do in one stream could have taken me months to cultivate,” he said. Piker has all the while become a central focus of Republican attacks. A recent push poll in Georgia attempted to tie Piker to the Democratic US senator Jon Ossoff, a rising star in the party. The pair have not campaigned together once. At this month’s Republican convention, Piker proved an unlikely star, with speakers frequently citing him as the personification of a supposed communist and anti-Israel takeover of the Democratic party. Most of the 15 attenders interviewed by the Guardian had never heard of him. Even seasoned convention-goers were in the dark. Chris Daniel, 44, from Houston, Texas, who has attended every Republican convention since 2004, assumed that Piker must be a British political candidate. But after months of pillorying on the right, the name did resonate with some. AJ Louderback, a Texas state legislator, dismissed him in stark ideological terms as “just another radical Muslim”, and remarked: “He doesn’t stand for American values.” Republicans, and rightwing media, were expert at creating a “boogeyman”, Piker notes, from transgender athletes to migrant caravans. But the attack isn’t as salient when it’s a “rabble rouser, Twitch streamer, random entertainer guy”, he says. “There’s just chaos everywhere, and people are just going about their daily lives, trying to make sense of it all and trying to find some kind of peace and stability and prosperity,” adds Piker. “No one is saying it’s because of a Twitch streamer. I’m not top of mind for anybody.” A day in Piker’s world At Piker’s house, the day begins with coffee delivery and checking his friend group’s standings in their fantasy football league. Piker grabs a new Zyn before getting on camera to record a pop culture podcast he does with his friends called Fear&. His dog, a fluffy Tibetan mastiff named Kaya, sits outside the podcast recording room. After almost two hours of podcasting, Piker moves over to the room where he streams on Twitch for seven hours. Art from fans, mostly of Piker, lines the walls around him. He scrolls through news stories, tweets and an endless chat window. Today he launches into the interview with Axios, which he calls a “hit job”, and as the circus around the interview spreads, suggests he maybe shouldn’t have done it, or didn’t expect it to become a clip show, or shouldn’t have used the term “pound for pound”, but that it wasn’t the “end of the world”. Piker spends the majority of each day on camera. He even eats on camera, taking breaks to use the bathroom. He works out and streams – that’s basically it – although he does have friends, who are around much of the time. At any given time, about 25,000 to 30,000 people are viewing the stream. Most of those do not watch for the duration, according to Piker, who says between 300,000 and 500,000 unique visitors will tune in each hour. In the chat, viewers lob questions, praise and criticism. “baby wake up, a new hasan bad press tour,” one person writes in the chat. “Rare hasan L shouldn’t have done this interview,” says another. Today’s stream focuses heavily on Piker himself. After a full streaming shift, he’s not done talking. Piker heads from his home studio to a live taping of Lovett or Leave It, a show from the Pod Save America co-host Jon Lovett that broadcasts on MS Now. (At arrival, a security guard asks me if I’m Piker’s publicist. A publicist, the streamer reflects later, would tell him not to do any interviews, even with friendlier outlets, at this point – when his whole job, really, is “dealing with the media”.) In his opening remarks, Lovett jokes, “If Democrats lose the midterms, we should not have to wonder if it’s because of missing mail-in ballots,” after talking about Trump’s efforts to derail mail voting. “We should know, without a shadow of a doubt, that it is because of Hasan Piker.” “I denounce you,” Lovett declares to Piker as he walks out on stage, a jocular nod to the string of condemnations of Piker’s statements that have featured during this year’s midterm campaigns. Lovett thinks Piker has said some “very stupid and bad” things, but also that a lot of his words have been taken out of context. But, he asks, how does Piker view his responsibility, given his influence and proximity to candidates who he wants to win? It’s a question Piker seems to wrestle with throughout the day. Still, he tells Lovett at one point, “The idea that a Twitch streamer is supposed to be held to a higher standard than the president is such an insane phenomenon.” “They’re elevating my status as this super-serious political commentator and then campaign consultant, campaign surrogate, when I’ve never wanted to be that,” he adds. Afterward, fans approach Piker for photos. One person, he says later, asks how he puts up with so much hatred coming his way for saying what he believes. He is both “very stubborn” and “very mission-oriented”, he explains. Has he considered talking less? “No,” he replies. “I mean, I talk less, I say the same stuff. Still going to be a problem.” David Smith contributed reporting

webTitle: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of Hormuz

fields.headline: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of Hormuz
fields.trailText: US president is said to expect renewed strikes after the midterms
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump has said he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week and resume nuclear talks in return for the lifting of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports. “They made a proposal but I reject it,” the US president told reporters at the White House. The president was earlier said to be privately sceptical Iran would meet his demands to dismantle its nuclear programme, according to unnamed US officials cited by the Wall Street Journal. Trump has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms in the US, the newspaper reported. Meanwhile, on Friday evening, he published a post on his Truth Social platform with a graphic showing a map with the strait of Hormuz renamed as the “Trump Strait”. During a three-hour meeting at the UN general assembly in New York earlier this week, Iran had proposed reopening the strait, which would relieve pressure on global energy markets, and restart talks on its nuclear programme within seven days. In return, as well as lifting its naval blockade, Iran wants the US to permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports and observe a “ceasefire on all fronts”. That would involve the US president convincing Israel to end its attacks on Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon, a tall order, and allowing the strait to reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, on Sunday said “our conditions are clear and any move toward reopening the strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled”. “We will not back down from them,” Araghchi said, state broadcaster IRIB reported. “We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights.” Reports of the rejection came as Iranian state media reported on Saturday morning that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, was on his way back to Tehran from New York. After a meeting with UN secretary general, António Guterres, Pezeshkian said: “Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table, but given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States.” Araghchi said on Sunday that the Iranians “saw the first reaction from the US president, but so far, nothing has been conveyed to us by the mediators”. “We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive positions to us, and we will make a decision based on them,” the foreign minister added. Earlier, a US official had ⁠said discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive” and, on Friday, Araghchi, had detailed the proposal to reporters outside the UN security council. He said the seven-day timeline to open the strait and resume talks could start as soon as the US accepts Iran’s proposal. The initial steps would take about four to five days to complete, the strait would be opened on the sixth day and talks on the nuclear programme would start on the seventh day, he said. This would include a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium. The US naval blockade is putting intense pressure on the Iranian economy, while the seven-month-old conflict in the region has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and is increasing the cost of living around the globe. Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”. “Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”. Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed ‌to end the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli attacks. Since then the conflict has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging its already ailing economy. Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq were blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market. The violence in Yemen has prompted a new humanitarian crisis, the UN children’s agency said on Friday, reporting a rise in acute malnutrition among children. Trump has previously said he was in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hardliners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates such as Pezeshkian. Diplomatic efforts surrounding the UN general assembly underscored the global stakes in the conflict. Marina Dunbar contributed. With Reuters and AP
